Monday, 8:15. The nightly job failed, the revenue dashboard shows Friday's numbers, and three people ask you "what happened?". This is the moment where an analytics engineer is really useful. Not because they never make mistakes (everybody does), but because they can read an error, find the guilty file in two minutes, fix it without breaking something else, and ship the fix through the normal review process.
Until now you met errors by accident. In this chapter you create them

: nine small "bug files" break the practice project in nine different ways, and you learn to recognise each message at first sight. Then you learn where dbt keeps the details (the log file, the compiled SQL, the executed SQL), how to decide if a problem is a SQL problem or a dbt problem, how to fix it safely on a branch, and how
change the way dbt runs and reports.

For the exam, topic 3 ("Debugging data modeling errors") is a group of five objectives, and many questions are built the same way: a real-looking error message, and "what is the cause?", "where do you look?" or "which flag?". If you have seen the messages yourself, these questions become easy points.

Parse (read YAML and files; dbt parse): Parsing Error (YAML), Compilation Error (Jinja syntax, missing ref/source, duplicate names). 2. Compile (render Jinja, link the DAG; dbt compile, dbt ls): Compilation Error (unknown macro, missing var), Found a cycle (a “Dependency Error”). 3. Execute (send SQL to the warehouse; dbt run, dbt show): Runtime Error / Binder Error (DuckDB), Database Error (other warehouses), connection errors. 4. Check (data tests and unit tests; dbt test, dbt build): FAIL / WARN (the data breaks a rule).

blocks.alt: A decision tree to find the cause of an error. Did dbt stop before sending SQL (Parsing / Compilation Error, cycle)? Yes: a dbt problem in the files: fix YAML, Jinja, ref/source names; check with dbt parse and dbt ls. No: copy target/compiled/… into the warehouse console and run it. Does it fail too? Yes: a pure SQL problem: fix the SQL in the model (column, join, syntax); use dbt show to check. No, it works: a dbt problem around the SQL: read target/run and logs/dbt.log (materialization, ;, contract, hooks, permissions on the target schema, incremental filter, on_schema_change…).

c: Finding the bug is half of the work. The other half is to fix it
, and in a way that your team can review. A fix that you test only by "it runs on my laptop" is how one broken model becomes three broken dashboards.

A hospital does not test a new medicine on the patient in the operating room. It tests it in the laboratory first, a second doctor checks the results, and only then is it used. Your development schema is the laboratory, the pull request is the second doctor, and the production job is the operating room.
